claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Jiang et al., 2009).

claims.claim: DNGR-1 is a vertebrate-restricted innate immune receptor dedicated to DAMP recognition.
claims.source: We have previously identified DNGR-1 (also known as CLEC9A) as a vertebrate-restricted innate immune receptor dedicated to DAMP recognition (Sancho et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Sancho et al., 2009).

claims.claim: The DAMP recognised by DNGR-1 is F-actin.
claims.source: We and others subsequently found that the DAMP recognised by DNGR-1 is F-actin, the polymer of G-actin that provides higher eukaryotic cells with structural integrity (Ahrens et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Ahrens et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Actin is extremely conserved (90% identity between yeast and humans).
claims.source: Actin is an ideal DAMP given that it is extremely conserved (90% identity between yeast and humans) and highly abundant and ubiquitous within all eukaryotic cells but absent from extracellular fluids.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about actin conservation.

claims.claim: Actin is highly abundant and ubiquitous within all eukaryotic cells but absent from extracellular fluids.
claims.source: Actin is an ideal DAMP given that it is extremely conserved (90% identity between yeast and humans) and highly abundant and ubiquitous within all eukaryotic cells but absent from extracellular fluids.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about actin distribution.

claims.claim: The requirement for Upd3 rules out the possibility that actin serves as a direct ligand for Domeless.
claims.source: The requirement for Upd3 rules out the possibility that actin serves as a direct ligand for Domeless, a conclusion further supported by the fact that actin does not induce TotM upregulation in various Drosophila cell lines that respond to Upd cytokines in vitro (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the genetic requirement for Upd3 and supported by in vitro data.

claims.claim: Actin does not induce TotM upregulation in various Drosophila cell lines that respond to Upd cytokines in vitro.
claims.source: The requirement for Upd3 rules out the possibility that actin serves as a direct ligand for Domeless, a conclusion further supported by the fact that actin does not induce TotM upregulation in various Drosophila cell lines that respond to Upd cytokines in vitro (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text as unpublished data.

claims.claim: Upd3 is synthesised by fat body cells that detect extracellular actin via a sensor(s) that couple(s) to a Nox-Src42A-Shark cascade.
claims.source: Therefore, the simplest interpretation of our data is that Upd3 is synthesised by fat body cells that detect extracellular actin via a sensor(s) that couple(s) to a Nox-Src42A-Shark cascade (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental data and depicted in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In Drosophila responses to wounding and in the clearance of axonal debris and neuronal cell corpses, Draper is phosphorylated by Src42A.
claims.source: Interestingly, in Drosophila responses to wounding and in the clearance of axonal debris and neuronal cell corpses, one such receptor is Draper, a member of the Nimrod family and orthologue of C. elegans Ced1. Draper contains an ITAM that is phosphorylated by Src42A (MacDonald et al., 2006; Ziegenfuss et al., 2008; Razzell et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (MacDonald et al., 2006; Ziegenfuss et al., 2008; Razzell et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The fly response to extracellular actin is elicited equally by G- and F-actin.
claims.source: In contrast to DNGR-1 dependent recognition, the fly response to extracellular actin is elicited equally by G- and F-actin, does not require phagocytes but the fat body and its function is not to prime adaptive immunity, which is absent in invertebrates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2k and 2l.

claims.claim: The fly response to extracellular actin does not require phagocytes but the fat body.
claims.source: In contrast to DNGR-1 dependent recognition, the fly response to extracellular actin is elicited equally by G- and F-actin, does not require phagocytes but the fat body and its function is not to prime adaptive immunity, which is absent in invertebrates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing haemocytes are dispensable (Figure 5) and the fat body is required (Figures 3 and 4).

claims.claim: The function of the fly response to extracellular actin is not to prime adaptive immunity, which is absent in invertebrates.
claims.source: In contrast to DNGR-1 dependent recognition, the fly response to extracellular actin is elicited equally by G- and F-actin, does not require phagocytes but the fat body and its function is not to prime adaptive immunity, which is absent in invertebrates.
claims.evidence: This is based on the established knowledge that invertebrates lack adaptive immunity.

claims.claim: The fly response to extracellular actin is coupled to production of Upd3 cytokine, which acts in an autocrine and paracrine manner to induce Domeless signalling via STAT.
claims.source: Rather, it is coupled to production of Upd3 cytokine, which acts in an autocrine and paracrine manner to induce Domeless signalling via STAT and to cause the induction of STAT-responsive genes, the products of which are released into the haemolymph.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: The Drosophila fat body response to actin results in secretion into the haemolymph of proteins that may regulate multiple aspects of fly physiology.
claims.source: Similarly, the Drosophila fat body response to actin results in secretion into the haemolymph of proteins that may regulate multiple aspects of fly physiology that coordinately impact resistance or tolerance to insult.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the known functions of STAT target genes and the analogy to the mammalian acute phase response.

claims.claim: Some components of the extracellular actin-sensing circuitry are conserved between flies and mammals (Shark, Src42A and ROS), while others are not (DNGR1, cross-presentation, dendritic cells).
claims.source: However, it is important to note that while some components of the extracellular actin-sensing circuitry are conserved between flies and mammals (Shark, Src42A and ROS), others are not (DNGR1, cross-presentation, dendritic cells).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the fly and mammalian systems.

claims.claim: DAMPs can be more conserved than their receptors or the responses they evoke.
claims.source: These differences suggest that DAMPs can be more conserved than their receptors or the responses they evoke.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that actin is conserved but the receptors and responses differ between flies and mammals.

claims.claim: The JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila can be induced by mechanical pressure, heat shock, dehydration, cytopathic infection, septic wounds and other traumas.
claims.source: The JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila can be induced by mechanical pressure, heat shock, dehydration, cytopathic infection, septic wounds and other traumas (Ekengren et al., 2001; Agaisse et al., 2003; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Dostert et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Ekengren et al., 2001; Agaisse et al., 2003; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Dostert et al., 2005).

claims.claim: A common denominator in all stimuli that induce JAK/STAT is cell death.

claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all JAK/STAT-inducing stimuli cause cell death, and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Actin is a potent DAMP for triggering the JAK/STAT pathway.
claims.source: Our data support that notion and suggest that actin is a potent DAMP for triggering the JAK/STAT pathway.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing actin induces JAK/STAT activation.

claims.source: Despite being commonly used as a marker of STAT activation, the function of Tot and Tep proteins in Drosophila is unknown. Nevertheless, genetic loss-of-function studies have implicated JAK/STAT signaling in resistance and/or tolerance to viral, bacterial and parasitoid infections (Yang et al., 2015; Agaisse et al., 2003; Agaisse and Perrimon, 2004; Brun et al., 2006; Dostert et al., 2005; Lamiable et al., 2016; Chakrabarti et al., 2016; Kemp et al., 2013; Merkling et al., 2015).

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Nam et al., 2012; Takeishi et al., 2013; Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Evans et al., 2015; Razzell et al., 2013).

results.result: Actin injection into Drosophila melanogaster induces selective expression of STAT target genes, including TotM, TotA, TotC, Socs36E, Diedel, and Tep1, without inducing antimicrobial peptide genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C10-C15, and C22 collectively demonstrate that actin injection triggers a sterile inflammatory response characterized by selective STAT target gene induction. The RNAseq data (C10, C11, C13), GSEA analysis (C13), bioinformatics validation (C14), RT-qPCR confirmation (C15), and absence of AMP induction (C16) provide converging evidence for this specific transcriptional response.

results.result: The actin-induced response is distinct from septic injury responses and does not require microbial contaminants, microbiota, or Wolbachia.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 demonstrate that actin induces a unique sterile inflammatory response. The absence of AMP gene induction (C16, C17), equivalent responses in germ-free and SPF flies (C20), independence from Wolbachia (C21), and greater TotM induction compared to other stimuli (C19) collectively support the specificity and sterile nature of the response.

results.result: The actin-induced response is physiologically relevant, conserved across species, and triggered by both G-actin and F-actin forms.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 establish the physiological relevance and mechanistic basis of actin sensing. The low dose requirement (C23), cross-species conservation (C24), and equivalent responses to G-actin and F-actin (C25, C26) are all supported by dose-response data and experiments with stabilized actin forms and non-polymerizable mutants.

results.result: STAT activation occurs in the fat body and is mediated through the JAK/STAT pathway via Domeless receptor.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C33 demonstrate that the fat body is the primary site of STAT activation. Tissue dissection (C27), reporter imaging (C28), and genetic manipulations using dominant-negative Domeless (C29, C30), dPIAS overexpression (C31), and STAT92E knockdown (C32) all converge to show that canonical JAK/STAT signaling in the fat body accounts for the global response.

results.result: While STAT activation is a major outcome of actin injection, extracellular actin likely triggers additional signaling pathways beyond JAK/STAT.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 show that not all actin-induced transcriptional changes are STAT-dependent. The observation that some upregulated genes are STAT-independent (C34) while some downregulated genes require STAT (C35) supports the conclusion that additional pathways are involved (C36). This is appropriately presented as a limitation of the STAT-centric model.

results.result: Fat body-derived Upd3, rather than haemocyte-derived Upd3, is required for the actin-induced STAT response.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 demonstrate a paradigm shift from the established role of haemocyte-derived Upd3. Haemocyte ablation experiments (C38), haemocyte-specific Upd3 knockdown (C39), fat body-specific Upd3 knockdown (C40), and specificity for Upd3 over Upd1/2 (C41) collectively support an autocrine/paracrine Upd3 loop in the fat body (C42).

results.result: The actin-induced response requires Shark and Src42A signaling specifically in the fat body.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 and C52 demonstrate that Shark (Drosophila Syk orthologue) and Src42A are essential for the response. Multiple genetic approaches including ubiquitous and fat body-specific knockdowns (C43-C46), dominant-negative overexpression (C47), and constitutively active Src42A (C48) provide strong converging evidence for the requirement of these kinases in the fat body.

results.result: Draper is not required for the actin-induced response in the fat body.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 demonstrate that despite initial observations in drpr null mutants (C49), Draper is not specifically required for the actin response. The lack of complementation rescue (C50) and absence of effect with fat body-specific knockdown (C51) indicate that the initial observation was due to a non-specific genetic background effect rather than Draper function.

results.result: The actin-induced response requires Nox-dependent ROS generation in the fat body, but not Duox.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 establish the role of oxidative signaling. Sod overexpression reducing the response (C55), lack of effect from Duox knockdown (C56), complete abrogation with Nox knockdown (C57), and the proposed mechanism linking Nox to Src42A activation (C58) collectively support a Nox-specific ROS requirement. The mechanistic model is appropriately presented as a suggestion based on the data.

results.result: Septic injury leads to actin release into haemolymph and Nox/Src42A-dependent TotM induction without affecting AMP expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 connect the actin-sensing pathway to physiological infection. Western blot detection of actin in haemolymph after septic injury (C60), TotM induction (C61), partial reduction with Nox knockdown (C62), complete abrogation with Src42A knockdown (C63), and specificity for STAT targets over AMPs (C64) support the possibility that released actin contributes to JAK/STAT activation during infection (C65).

results.result: In mammals, actin is recognized as a DAMP by DNGR-1, which signals through Src-family kinases and Syk to promote DC cross-presentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C89-C90 describe established prior work on mammalian actin recognition. These claims are supported by citations to the authors' previous publications and are presented as background context for the current study. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.

results.result: Extracellular actin detection via Src-family kinase and Syk-dependent signaling is evolutionarily conserved, though specific receptors and responses differ between flies and mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 and C102-C103 present the main conceptual conclusion of the manuscript. The experimental demonstration that Shark (Syk orthologue), Src42A, and ROS are required in flies, combined with the known role of Syk and Src in mammalian DNGR-1 signaling, supports the conservation of signaling components. The acknowledgment that receptors and responses differ (C102, C103) appropriately qualifies the evolutionary conservation claim.

results.result: The Drosophila actin response differs from mammalian DNGR-1 signaling in that it is triggered by both G- and F-actin, requires the fat body rather than phagocytes, and functions through Upd3/Domeless/STAT rather than adaptive immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 highlight key mechanistic differences between fly and mammalian systems. The equal responsiveness to G- and F-actin (C97), requirement for fat body rather than haemocytes (C98), and coupling to Upd3/STAT signaling (C100) are all supported by experimental data. The statement about adaptive immunity (C99) is based on established knowledge.

results.result: Src family kinases are redox-sensitive and can be activated by NADPH oxidase-derived ROS in response to wounding, as shown in zebrafish and Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 and C113-C114 describe established mechanisms from prior work that provide context for the current findings. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to the literature and establish the precedent for ROS-mediated Src activation that the authors invoke to explain their Nox/Src42A results.

results.result: Background on sterile inflammation, DAMPs, and the Drosophila immune system, including the JAK/STAT pathway and its activation by stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C88 provide extensive background information on sterile inflammation, DAMPs, Drosophila immunity, and JAK/STAT signaling. These claims are well-supported by citations to the literature and accurately represent established knowledge in the field. They provide essential context for interpreting the experimental findings.

results.result: Actin is highly conserved (90% identity between yeast and humans) and is abundant within cells but absent from extracellular fluids.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 state well-established facts about actin that justify its potential as a universal DAMP. These claims are based on general knowledge in cell biology and are accurate.

results.result: Actin does not directly activate Domeless; instead, an unknown sensor in fat body cells detects actin and couples to the Nox-Src42A-Shark cascade to induce Upd3 production.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 present a mechanistic model based on genetic epistasis experiments and in vitro data. The requirement for Upd3 (C93), lack of direct TotM induction in cell lines (C94), and the proposed model (C95) are appropriately presented as inferences from the data. The model acknowledges the unknown nature of the actin sensor.

results.result: In Drosophila wound healing and debris clearance, Draper is phosphorylated by Src42A.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 describes established prior work on Draper signaling that provides context for why the authors tested Draper's role in actin sensing. This claim is well-supported by citations to the literature.

results.result: The JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila is induced by diverse stresses that share cell death as a common feature, and actin is a potent DAMP for triggering this pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 synthesize prior knowledge (C104) with an inference about the common mechanism (C105) and the current findings (C106). The conclusion that actin is a potent DAMP for JAK/STAT activation (C106) is well-supported by the experimental data, and the speculation about cell death as a common denominator (C105) is appropriately presented as an inference.

results.result: Actin released into insect haemolymph during infection can act as both a direct antimicrobial agent and an indirect activator of JAK/STAT responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 cite prior work showing actin release and antimicrobial activity during infection. Claim C109 integrates this with the current findings to propose a dual function for released actin. This synthesis is appropriately presented as an inference and is consistent with both the cited literature and the experimental data.

results.result: JAK/STAT signaling has been implicated in resistance/tolerance to infections and intestinal homeostasis, though the functional significance of induced STAT target genes during infection remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 summarize prior work on JAK/STAT function in Drosophila. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations and provide context for the authors' unsuccessful attempts to identify a functional role for actin-induced STAT activation (mentioned in the Discussion but not extracted as explicit claims).

results.result: The Drosophila fat body response to actin may regulate multiple aspects of fly physiology through secreted proteins, analogous to the mammalian acute phase response.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 proposes a functional analogy to the mammalian acute phase response. While the analogy is reasonable given the fat body's role as a liver equivalent and the secretion of STAT target gene products, the authors acknowledge in the Discussion that they were unable to demonstrate functional consequences of actin-induced STAT activation in various challenge models. This limits the support for the proposed physiological significance.
